items.title: Jasper Taylor Interview, 1959-06-30
items.q: Handy was the leader of the new ones, and Harry Mestrels, and they went to Cuba in 1906 or something like that.

ctx.x: They always call that Shake It and Break It. They still do down there. They speak of it, they have the words they sing about Shake It and Break It, hang it on the wall. So they still call that tune the Shake It and Break It quite often.

Now here's something that is important, very important, uh, I think, uh, I've often asked myself, where did Handy get the Spanish beat in St. Louis Blues? Yeah, I know what you mean. I often wondered why he, why, why, why, then Robert Campbell told me last week that Handy was in Cuba with the Meharry Mestrels. And that Lucille Handy, his oldest daughter was, I, he said that, uh, was born in Cuba. I never heard Handy say that out of the years that I was associated with him. But Robert Campbell, who was closer than…

trumpet for Handy back in those days, and as a great Handy fan, and before Handy passed, he called him in to be a witness on his will. And I saw him in the hospital here last week, and he gave me that information, which I did not know. That Handy was the leader of the new ones, and Harry Mestrels, and they went to Cuba in 1906 or something like that. So we, so I just, it's just an idea of mine, and probably he got that beat from over there.
